myths.Agent_1:
Long ago, before the ages of men, the brilliant sun and the pale moon shared the sky equally, side by side. During this golden age, the Owl was the most magnificent bird of all, boasting feathers of pure, radiant gold. He was the Sun’s favored messenger, tasked with carrying the morning light to the corners of the earth.

But the Owl grew vain. He believed his golden plumage was the true source of the daylight, not the Sun. One evening, he refused to lower his wings to let the Moon begin her watch, declaring that the world belonged only to his brilliance.

Angered by this arrogance, the Sun reached down and stripped the Owl of his golden fire. His feathers faded to dull browns and greys, blending with the bark of the trees. To teach him humility, the Sun banished him from the day entirely.

Since then, the Owl has been condemned to the night. He hides in the dense, silent shadows of the ancient forest, deeply ashamed of his lost splendor. He only speaks to ask "Who?" into the darkness, forever searching for the glorious creature he once was, punished to watch the Moon he once tried to outshine.
myths.Agent_2:
Long before early humans walked the earth, the towering mountains were completely silent. This was the domain of Aethon, the Keeper of Sound. Aethon was a solitary spirit who believed that noise was a precious treasure, too fragile to be left wandering the peaks. Whenever a stone fell, a river splashed, or the wind howled, Aethon would catch the sound in a delicate crystal jar and store it deep within his dark cavern.

For millennia, the world above was deafeningly quiet. But one evening, a mischievous wind spirit named Zephyr grew bored of the silence. She sneaked into Aethon’s cavern, swirling through the endless rows of glowing crystal jars. With a sudden, careless gust, Zephyr knocked a single jar from its pedestal. It shattered, releasing a booming crash that knocked over another jar, and then another.

A chain reaction of shattering glass echoed through the cave, releasing millions of trapped sounds at once. The cacophony blew the cavern roof apart, scattering the sounds into the vast, open world. Now without a home, these orphaned sounds hide in canyons and valleys. Whenever a traveler calls out, the sounds eagerly mimic the noise, hoping to finally be captured and brought home again.

myths.Agent_2:
Myth: Long before men walked the earth, the night sky was entirely pitch black, devoid of the twinkling stars and vibrant hues we know today. This was the doing of Kaelen, the selfish Weaver of Light. Kaelen believed that the brilliant colors of the cosmos were too majestic for the mortal realm. Whenever a comet flared or a nebula bloomed, Kaelen would snatch the vibrant ribbons of light from the heavens and weave them into glowing tapestries, hiding them inside his celestial tent.

For millennia, the world below suffered in absolute, terrifying darkness. But one evening, a curious frost fox named Vix, desperate for warmth in the freezing void, sneaked into Kaelen’s tent. Mesmerized by the endless rows of radiant fabrics, Vix playfully tugged at a loose, shimmering thread.

The thread unraveled with a sharp snap, tearing the grandest tapestry in two. A torrent of trapped light burst forth, sweeping Vix up in a brilliant, chaotic storm. The swirling colors shattered the tent, bleeding out into the harsh northern winds. Today, these orphaned lights forever dance across the polar skies. The Aurora Borealis is simply the little frost fox, endlessly scattering Kaelen's hoarded colors across the cold, dark, freezing winter night.
myths.Agent_1:
Myth: Long before the ages of men, the brilliant Sun and the pale Moon shared the sky. During this era, the great Moth was the most magnificent creature, boasting wings woven from the Sun’s pure, liquid light. He was the Sun’s favored herald, carrying the dawn across the horizon.

But the Moth grew vain. He believed his glowing wings were the true source of daylight. One evening, he refused to fold his wings to let the Moon begin her watch, declaring that the sky belonged only to his brilliance.

Angered by this arrogance, the Moon called upon the fierce night winds. The winds swirled around the Moth, tearing the liquid light from his wings and shattering it into thousands of tiny, glowing fragments. His beautiful wings faded to a dull, ashen grey, blending with the shadows of the dusk.

The shattered fragments of his former glory were scattered across the forests and meadows, becoming the very first fireflies. Since then, the grey Moth has been condemned to the night. He flutters endlessly in the dark, forever chasing after those tiny, drifting sparks of light, desperately trying to gather the shattered pieces of his stolen brilliance.

myths.Agent_1:
Myth: Long before the ages of men, the cosmos was guarded by a colossal Serpent. During this ancient era, the Serpent was the most magnificent creature of the heavens, boasting scales woven from pure, crystallized starlight. He was the night’s favored sentinel, wrapping his glowing body across the dark sky to form the shimmering Milky Way.

But the Serpent grew vain. He believed his starry scales were far more beautiful than the daylight. One morning, he refused to uncoil and let the Sun rise, declaring that the heavens belonged entirely to his brilliant silver coils.

Angered by this arrogance, the Sun flared with an intense, blazing heat. The golden fire scorched the Serpent, shattering his crystallized scales into thousands of tiny, burning fragments. His radiant body faded to a dull, dusty brown, suddenly heavy and bound to the earth below.

The shattered fragments of his former glory plummeted through the atmosphere, becoming the very first meteor showers. Since then, the Serpent has been condemned to crawl upon the dirt. He hides in the shadows of the rocks, forever shedding his skin, desperately hoping that beneath the dull surface, his stolen coat of magnificent starlight will finally grow back.
myths.Agent_2:
Myth: Long before humans walked the earth, the sprawling forests were completely devoid of color, painted only in monotonous shades of green and brown. This dreary world was the doing of Ignis, the greedy Keeper of Autumn. Ignis believed that the vibrant sparks of the season—the fiery reds, bright oranges, and golden yellows—were too magnificent for the ordinary trees. Whenever a leaf dared to change color, Ignis would snatch the vivid spark and hoard it inside his colossal, hollow oak.

For millennia, the woods remained dull and unchanging. But one afternoon, a drab, curious squirrel named Bramble, desperate to find a hidden cache of acorns, sneaked into Ignis’s colossal oak. Mesmerized by the swirling pool of glowing, liquid colors, Bramble accidentally knocked over a massive wooden basin.

The basin tipped with a resounding crack, spilling a tidal wave of vibrant, fiery hues out of the tree. The rushing river of color swept through the forest, splashing against the canopy and soaking into the leaves. Today, this annual flood of color sweeps across the globe. Autumn is simply the lingering magic of that spilled basin, as Bramble's clumsy mistake forever paints the world in breathtaking fire before winter arrives.

Myth: Long before humans walked the earth, the early mornings were completely dry and harsh, offering no relief to the parched land. This arid world was the doing of Maris, the greedy Warden of Dew. Maris believed that the shimmering, crystalline drops of morning moisture were far too precious for the ordinary grass and flowers. Whenever a silver drop tried to form, Maris would snatch the liquid gem and hoard it inside his colossal, floating cloud chalice.

For millennia, the dawns remained barren and dusty. But one morning, a tiny, thirsty swallow named Pip, desperate to find a single drop of water, sneaked onto Maris’s floating cloud. Mesmerized by the swirling pool of glowing, silver liquid, Pip fluttered too close and accidentally knocked over the massive chalice.

The chalice tipped with a booming thunderclap, spilling a tidal wave of shimmering mist down upon the world. The rushing river of silver swept over the meadows, splashing against the petals and soaking into the blades of grass. Today, this daily gift of moisture blankets the globe. Morning dew is simply the lingering magic of that spilled chalice, as Pip's clumsy mistake forever paints the world in breathtaking, sparkling silver before the golden sunrise.

During this ancient era, the Whale was the most magnificent creature of the heavens, boasting a hide woven from pure, shimmering rainbows. He was the sky’s favored guardian, swimming through the clouds to form the brilliant arcs of light after every storm.

He breaches the surface endlessly, singing mournful songs to the cold, empty sky, desperately hoping that his stolen coat of magnificent rainbows will finally return to him.

Myth: Long before the earliest ages of men, the frozen northern mountains were patrolled by a colossal Wolf. During this ancient era, the Wolf was the most magnificent creature of the peaks, boasting a thick coat woven from pure, crackling lightning. He was the storm’s favored guardian, sprinting across the clouds to ignite brilliant flashes during every tempest.

But the Wolf grew vain. He believed his electric silver fur was far more powerful than the gentle warmth of spring. One morning, he refused to stop his tempest and let the snows melt, declaring that the earth belonged entirely to his roaring, endless winter.

Angered by this arrogance, the Sun struck him with a searing beam of golden heat. The radiant blast scorched the Wolf, shattering his lightning coat into thousands of tiny, glowing sparks. His towering body faded to a dull, heavy grey, suddenly bound to the forests below.

The shattered fragments of his former glory drifted through the summer air, becoming the first fireflies. Since then, the Wolf has been condemned to roam the woods. He points his snout upward, howling mournfully to the empty sky, desperately hoping that his stolen coat of magnificent lightning will finally return to him.
myths.Agent_2:
Myth: Long before humans walked the earth, the summer nights were completely pitch black, offering no guiding light beneath the dense forest canopy. This dark world was the doing of Noctis, the greedy Keeper of Twilight. Noctis believed that the glowing, golden embers of dusk were far too precious for the ordinary woods and meadows. Whenever a speck of light tried to linger, he would snatch the radiant spark and hoard it inside his colossal, hollow obsidian lantern.

For millennia, the midnight woods remained shrouded and perilous. But one evening, a tiny, lost moth named Luna, desperate to find a single spark of warmth, sneaked into his deep cavern. Mesmerized by the swirling pool of glowing, golden light, Luna fluttered too close and accidentally knocked over the massive lantern.

The lantern tipped with a resounding crash, shattering into pieces and spilling a tidal wave of shimmering sparks out into the world. The rushing river of gold swept through the trees, splashing against the bushes and taking flight. Today, this nightly gift of light dances across the globe. Fireflies are simply the lingering magic of that shattered lantern, as Luna's clumsy mistake forever paints the world in breathtaking, sparkling gold before dawn.

Myth: Long before the earliest ages of men, the endless, frozen tundras were roamed by a colossal Stag. During this ancient era, the Stag was the most magnificent creature of the wild, boasting towering antlers woven from pure, crystallized aurora. He was the winter’s favored sentinel, striding across the snowdrifts to provide a brilliant, glowing beacon for wandering spirits in the long polar night.

But the Stag grew vain. He believed his luminescent, shifting colors were far more beautiful than the vibrant greens of spring. One year, he refused to let the frost melt to allow the changing of seasons, declaring that the earth belonged entirely to his crisp, shimmering winter.

Angered by this arrogance, the Earth Mother struck him with a piercing shaft of vernal warmth. The sudden heat scorched the Stag, shattering his auroral antlers into thousands of tiny, gleaming fragments. His colossal body faded to a dull, earthy brown, suddenly bound to the dense, shadowy forests.

The shattered fragments of his former glory sank into the soil, becoming the very first glowing fire opals. Since then, the Stag has been condemned to wander the woods. He scrapes his dull bone antlers against ancient trees, desperately hoping his stolen crown of magnificent light will finally return to him.

Myth: Long before the age of men, the towering mountain peaks were ruled by a colossal Eagle. During this ancient era, the Eagle was the most magnificent creature of the skies, boasting massive wings woven entirely from rolling thunderclouds and crackling purple lightning. He was the sky’s favored harbinger, soaring across the valleys to provide the rushing rains that nourished the spring blossoms.

But the Eagle grew vain. He believed his booming storms were far more beautiful than the quiet, golden warmth of summer. One year, he refused to let the heavy rains pass, declaring that the heavens belonged entirely to his deafening thunder.

Angered by this arrogance, the Sun God struck him with a piercing shaft of absolute light. The brilliant beam scorched the Eagle, shattering his tempestuous wings into thousands of tiny, gleaming sparks. His colossal body shrank to a dull, heavy brown, suddenly bound to the ordinary thermal drafts.

The shattered fragments of his former glory scattered into the evening air, becoming the very first glowing fireflies. Since then, the Eagle is condemned to wander the mundane skies. He screeches desperately at the empty blue heavens, hoping his stolen wings of magnificent lightning will finally return to him.
